actual_assessment:
Provisional preference: T, ‘When the whole earth rejoices, I will make you desolate.’ If T is already retained, retain it. Replacing P with T would materially improve temporal fidelity; replacing M with T would favor the less inferential assignment of agency, while losing M’s explicit connection with verse 15.

The contract’s SHA256 matches the supplied frozen hash. I inspected only that contract and its two permitted GKC pages. This is one bounded assessment, with a reverse-order check, not two independent votes.

First presentation order, M → T → P:

M: Edom rejoiced previously over the whole land; God’s coming judgment corresponds to that rejoicing. ‘You’ is supplied as the infinitive’s subject, ‘the whole land’ becomes its object, and ‘over’ expresses the inferred relation. The comparative ‘just as’ anticipates verse 15’s explicit retaliation formula. This gives verses 10–15 a coherent movement from Edom’s territorial claims and hostility to recompense. Its principal weakness is the accumulation of interpretive decisions within verse 14: the subject is unstated, the following noun is construed as object, and the joy is placed in the past. The context supports those decisions collectively, but does not compel them. Nor does the general possibility of infinitive objects establish this particular verb’s construction.

T: The whole earth rejoices at the time of Edom’s coming desolation; the occasion or object of its joy remains unspecified. It reads the following noun phrase as subject and takes kaf temporally. A following subject is an ordinary infinitive construction, though object constructions and contextually supplied subjects also exist (GKC 115). Temporal kaf and contextually determined infinitive time make this rendering available without changing the Hebrew (GKC 114). Verse 14 then juxtaposes general rejoicing with Edom’s desolation; verse 15 explains the fitting retaliation for Edom’s earlier rejoicing. ‘Earth’ rather than ‘land’ remains a consequential lexical choice. T must not be expanded to say that the earth rejoices because Edom falls or because Israel is restored: neither occasion is explicit here.

P: The whole earth rejoiced previously, over an unspecified object, and Edom will subsequently become desolate. Its subject assignment is straightforward, but its past tense needs contextual justification. An infinitive can refer to past action; consequently, P is not disqualified simply because the Hebrew is infinitival. The difficulty is that the supplied context explicitly locates Edom’s rejoicing in the past, not the whole earth’s. English ‘as’ also leaves readers wavering between comparison, temporal relation, and cause. P preserves lexical ambiguity in the conjunction while imposing a poorly supported temporal separation.

Strongest counterargument to T: M gives verse 14 a direct anticipatory relationship to verse 15, and the surrounding accusations supply Edom as a plausible unexpressed subject. T’s apparently straightforward syntax cannot establish that this contextual interpretation is wrong. Nevertheless, under the contract’s priority for agency and unsupported additions, T asks the reader to supply less.

Reverse presentation order, P → T → M: P still lacks a clear contextual basis for past worldwide rejoicing; T still gives the most economical subject-and-time reading; M remains the strongest contextual competitor. The preference is unchanged. This order check adds no independent evidential weight.

Recommended reader disclosure: Or, ‘Just as you rejoiced over the whole land, I will make you desolate,’ taking Edom as the implied subject in light of verse 15. The Hebrew can also mean ‘the whole land’ where the translation reads ‘the whole earth’; the occasion of the rejoicing is not stated.

Unlisted alternative worth a separate bounded comparison: ‘As the whole earth rejoices, I will make you desolate.’ It may preserve more of kaf’s flexibility than T, but English ‘as’ can introduce an unintended causal implication. I do not find it demonstrably stronger on this assessment and would not silently substitute it.

This judgment concerns the retained Hebrew joy/judgment clause only. It establishes neither literary-edition priority nor historical original wording, and does not certify the divine-title formula or verse 15’s English.
